about.titleLine2: at the edge of the sand.
about.lead: Dunes Insolites runs out of Sabria, a village on the last road before the Grand Erg Oriental. Everyone who guides for us grew up within sight of these dunes.
about.whyP1: Most desert trips in Tunisia are sold by the busload — forty people, one camel line, twenty minutes, back on the coach. We wanted the opposite: small groups, local guides, and enough time on the sand that the desert stops being a photo stop and starts being a place.
about.whyP2: So we run a maximum of twelve guests per departure, twice a day, from a gate ten minutes south of Douz. Every trip is timed around the light — out before the heat, or out as the sun starts to drop.
about.how1: Every guide is from Sabria, Douz, or Kebili, and paid year-round, not per trip.
about.how2: Groups cap at twelve, and we never merge two bookings to fill a departure.
about.how3: Camels work a maximum of two trips a day and rest the whole summer.
about.how4: We carry out everything we carry in — the camps leave no trace by morning.
about.how5: A share of every booking funds the Sabria school's water tank.
about.guide1Bio: Born in Sabria, raised on the dune belt. Hédi started with two camels and a pot of tea in 2018 and still leads the golden-hour caravan most evenings.
about.guide2Bio: Former rally mechanic. Yasmine sets every route in the sand sea, briefs every rider, and keeps the fleet in better shape than most road cars.
about.guide3Bio: Snowboarder turned dune rider. Karim can have someone who has never stood on a board carving a face inside ten minutes, and he films the proof.

story.title: An adventure born from our passion for the desert

safety.title: Safety in the sand.
safety.lead: The Sahara is forgiving if you respect it and unforgiving if you don't. Here is exactly how we run our trips.
safety.onEveryTrip1: A licensed lead guide, plus a sweep guide on any group of six or more.
safety.onEveryTrip2: Radio contact with the gate base and a satellite messenger per group.
safety.onEveryTrip3: A first-aid kit, shade sheet, and twice the water we expect anyone to drink.
safety.onEveryTrip4: Helmets, goggles, and gloves issued and checked for every quad rider.
safety.onEveryTrip5: Boards, bindings, and saddles inspected between every session.
safety.heatProtocolBody: From June to September we run only the early morning and the last hour before sunset. If the forecast at the gate reads above 44°C we stand the day down and everyone is refunded or rebooked, no questions and no fee.
safety.insuranceP1: We carry public liability cover for all guided activity. That does not replace your own travel insurance — check that yours covers quad riding and sandboarding, since some policies class them as extreme sports.
safety.insuranceP2: The nearest hospital is in Douz, twelve minutes from the gate. Every vehicle in our fleet can reach it directly from anywhere on our routes.
safety.bring1: Closed shoes you don't mind filling with sand
safety.bring2: Long sleeves and long trousers — sun, not modesty
safety.bring4: A layer for after dark; the desert drops fast once the sun is down
safety.bring5: Cash for tips if you want to; cards work at the gate for everything else
safety.faqQ1: Do I need experience to ride a quad?
safety.faqA1: No. The quads are automatic and every session starts with a briefing and a practice lap on the flat before we head into the dunes. Riders must be 16 or older and carry ID.
safety.faqQ2: Is the camel trek suitable for children?
safety.faqA2: Children from six can ride with a parent, and handlers walk beside every camel for the whole route. Below six we recommend the sunset camp visit instead — same tea, no saddle.
safety.faqQ3: What happens if the weather turns?
safety.faqA3: Sandstorms and high wind mean we cancel, and you get a full refund or a free reschedule. That call is made by the lead guide, never by the booking desk.
safety.faqA4: Closed shoes, long sleeves, and sunglasses. We hand out a chèche for your head and neck at the gate. Skip anything you would be upset to get sand into.
safety.faqQ5: Is there phone signal out there?
safety.faqA5: Patchy. Every guide carries a satellite messenger and a charged radio, and the base at the gate knows every route and expected return time.
safety.faqQ6: Can you handle dietary or medical needs?
safety.faqA6: Yes — tell us when you book. We cater vegetarian, vegan, and gluten-free at the camp, and our guides are briefed on any condition you share with us.
safety.ctaBody: Ask us anything before you book — we answer within a day, usually the same hour.

privacy.collectP1: When you book a trip we collect your name, email address, phone number, party size, chosen date and departure, and any pickup or dietary notes you give us. If you join the newsletter we store only your email address.
privacy.collectP2: Our servers log standard technical data — IP address, browser, and the pages you visited — for security and to keep the site working.
privacy.why1: To confirm, run, and if necessary reschedule your trip.
privacy.why2: To reach you if the weather forces a change.
privacy.why3: To meet our legal and accounting obligations in Tunisia.
privacy.why4: To send occasional trip news, only if you asked for it.
privacy.whoP: Your guide sees the details needed to run your trip. Beyond that we share data only with the providers that host our site, send our email, and process payments, and only as much as each needs. We never sell your data.
privacy.keepP: Booking records are kept for seven years, as Tunisian accounting law requires. Newsletter subscriptions are kept until you unsubscribe, which every email lets you do in one click.
privacy.rightsPre: You can ask us for a copy of your data, ask us to correct it, or ask us to delete anything we are not legally required to keep. Write to

privacy.cookiesP: We use a single functional cookie to remember your cookie choice. We do not run advertising trackers. If we add analytics we will ask first.

terms.title: Terms & conditions
terms.bookingP: A booking is a request until we confirm it by email with a reference number. Prices are per person in euros and include guiding, equipment, and transfers from Douz and Kebili unless stated otherwise on the trip page.
terms.paymentP: Nothing is charged when you book. We take payment at the gate before departure, or by secure link if you prefer to settle in advance. Cash in dinar and cards are both accepted.
terms.cancel1: Cancel more than 24 hours before departure: no charge.
terms.cancel2: Cancel within 24 hours: 50% of the trip price.
terms.cancel3: No-show at the gate: full price.
terms.cancel4: If we cancel — weather, equipment, or anything else on our side — you choose a full refund or a free reschedule.
terms.participationP1: Quad riders must be 16 or older and carry photo ID. Camel riders under six must ride with an adult. Tell us at booking about any medical condition, pregnancy, or mobility need so we can put you on the right trip — we would rather move you than turn you away at the gate.
terms.participationP2: Our guides may refuse or stop participation for anyone under the influence of alcohol or drugs, or anyone who ignores a safety instruction. No refund is due in that case.
terms.riskP: Desert activities carry inherent risk. We manage it with briefings, equipment checks, and trained guides, but we cannot remove it. You take part at your own risk and are responsible for holding travel insurance that covers these activities.
terms.liabilityP: We carry public liability insurance for guided activity. Nothing in these terms limits our liability for death or personal injury caused by our negligence. Otherwise our liability is limited to the price of the trip.
terms.photographyP: Guides photograph and film trips and send you the results. We also sometimes use those images publicly — tell your guide at the gate if you would rather we didn't, and we won't.
terms.lawPre: These terms are governed by Tunisian law. Complaints go to
terms.lawPost: and we will answer within 14 days.

faqPage.title: Everything worth knowing before you book
faqPage.lead: Booking answers from our operating rules, plus destination facts checked against UNESCO and official Tunisian travel sources.
faqPage.a1: More than 24 hours before departure: no charge. Within 24 hours: 50% of the trip price. No-show at the gate: full price. If we're the ones cancelling — weather, equipment, or any reason on our side — you choose between a full refund or a free reschedule.
faqPage.q2: Do I pay when I book?
faqPage.a2: No. Nothing is charged at booking time — payment is taken at the gate or through a secure link.
faqPage.q3: What happens if the weather turns on the day of my trip?
faqPage.a3: Sandstorms and strong wind mean cancellation, with a full refund or a free reschedule. That call is made by the head guide, never by the booking office.
faqPage.q4: What should I wear and bring?
faqPage.a4: Closed shoes, long sleeves, and sunglasses for the day; a warm layer for the evening, since desert nights are cool even after a hot day. We hand out a chèche (head and neck scarf) at the gate.
faqPage.q5: Is there phone signal in Sabria?
faqPage.a5: Intermittent at best. Every guide carries a charged satellite messenger and radio, and the base at the gate knows every route and expected return time.
faqPage.q6: Can you handle dietary or medical needs?
faqPage.a6: Yes — tell us when you book. We offer vegetarian, vegan, and gluten-free options at the camp, and our guides are briefed on any condition you tell us about.
faqPage.q7: Do I need experience to drive a quad?
faqPage.a7: No. The quads are automatic, and every session starts with a briefing and a practice lap on flat ground before heading into the dunes. Drivers must be 16 or older with photo ID.
faqPage.q8: Is the camel trek suitable for children?
faqPage.a8: Children aged six and up can ride with a parent, with a camel handler walking alongside each camel the whole way. Under six, we recommend the sunset camp visit instead.
faqPage.q9: What about pregnancy or a mobility need?
faqPage.a9: Tell us when you book — we'd much rather point you to the right trip than turn you away at the gate.
faqPage.catDestination: Getting here and understanding the region
faqPage.q10: Can I arrive in my own vehicle or request a transfer?
faqPage.a10: Both options are supported in the booking flow. Choose your own vehicle or an available transport option, then provide the requested pickup details. The team confirms the exact meeting or pickup point before departure.
faqPage.q11: What are a ksar and a ghorfa?
faqPage.a11: A ksar is a fortified collective granary; ksour is the plural. Its stacked storage chambers are called ghorfas. Around Tataouine and Medenine, these structures stored harvests and were tied to semi-nomadic life in the region.
faqPage.q12: Why visit Chenini and Tataouine rather than treating them as a photo stop?
faqPage.a12: The landscape tells a connected story: hilltop settlements, rock-cut homes, water-management systems and collective granaries. Chenini and nearby Douiret are living places, so a slower visit with local context is more respectful and more informative.
faqPage.q13: Is Djerba a UNESCO World Heritage site?
faqPage.a13: Yes. UNESCO inscribed Djerba in 2023 for its distinctive dispersed settlement pattern and the way communities adapted to a water-scarce island environment. The listed property is a series of sites and monuments, not a single building.
faqPage.q14: When is the best season for the Tunisian Sahara?
faqPage.a14: Tunisia's official tourism portal presents winter as the ideal season for exploring the Sahara and autumn as suitable for desert travel. Conditions vary by day, so check the forecast and follow the operating team's timing and weather decision.
faqPage.q15: Should I check official travel advice before a southern Tunisia trip?
faqPage.a15: Yes. Advice and restricted zones can change. Check the current guidance issued for your nationality, make sure your insurance covers the planned route and activities, and do not improvise travel into border or military zones.
faqPage.a16: The camp is in Sabria, in Tunisia's Kébili governorate, approximately 30 km from Douz according to the official Dunes Insolites presentation. The precise GPS point and arrival instructions are confirmed for your booking.
faqPage.q17: Can a normal family car reach the camp?
faqPage.a17: The official camp information says it is accessible by family car under normal conditions. Follow only the confirmed approach and contact the team if weather or sand has changed the track; do not improvise another route.
faqPage.q18: Are there showers and toilets at the camp?
faqPage.a18: Yes. The camp's official presentation lists on-site showers, including hot water, alongside its tent accommodation. The exact facilities attached to your chosen accommodation are shown during booking and confirmed by the team.
faqPage.q19: What kinds of nights can I book?
faqPage.a19: The catalogue distinguishes the established camp from a simpler bivouac deeper in the desert. At the fixed camp, accommodation options can include a traditional tent, room or suite depending on current availability.
faqPage.q20: What food is part of the Dunes Insolites experience?
faqPage.a20: The camp presents traditional meals prepared with regional products, mint tea and desert bread cooked with hot sand and embers. Your selected stay states what is included; dietary needs should be provided before confirmation.
faqPage.q21: Which activities can be added at Dunes Insolites?
faqPage.a21: The public camp information and current catalogue include camel outings, quad trips, sandboarding, horse experiences, sunset photography and desert bivouacs. Only activities actually available for your date appear or are confirmed for booking.
faqPage.q22: What is the difference between the fixed camp and a bivouac?
faqPage.a22: The fixed camp prioritises established accommodation and facilities. A bivouac is a simpler, more mobile night farther into the dunes. Choose according to the comfort level, travel time and programme described on the specific stay page.
faqPage.q23: Can families, private groups or events be accommodated?
faqPage.a23: Dunes Insolites publicly offers group activities and events, while the booking system records party size and special requests. Send the group's ages, dates and needs before confirmation so the team can propose a suitable programme rather than assume every activity fits everyone.
faqPage.q24: What happens after I send a booking request?
faqPage.a24: The website does not charge immediately. The request is checked against availability and the selected services; the local team then confirms the programme, arrival or pickup details and the next payment step by email or WhatsApp.
faqPage.sourcesNote: Operational answers come from the booking rules. Destination and heritage answers are checked against the following primary sources.

guideSahara.title: The Sabria desert, in the Tunisian Sahara
guideSahara.lead: Where the camp is, when to come, and what you can actually do there.
guideSahara.whereP1: Sabria sits in the Kébili governorate, at the edge of the Tunisian Sahara — the region that holds most of the country's desert, alongside Douz, Ksar Ghilane, Tozeur, Tataouine, and Matmata.
guideSahara.whereP2: That's where our camp is: traditional tents, camels, and quads, right at the line between the palm grove and the first dunes.
guideSahara.whenP1: The best window runs October through April: warm but manageable days, cool nights — exactly right for sleeping outdoors without suffering from heat or cold.
guideSahara.whenP2: July and August are worth avoiding: daytime temperatures regularly pass 40°C (104°F), which makes anything in direct sun hard going.
guideSahara.whatHeading: What there is to do in Sabria
guideSahara.whatP1: Three experiences make up most trips here: the camel trek, the quad safari, and dune sandboarding — each booked as an add-on to a night's stay or a bivouac.
guideSahara.whatP2: The stay itself comes in two shapes: the fixed camp, with a choice of accommodation (tent, room, or dune suite), or the bivouac, a simpler night further into the dunes.
guideSahara.practicalP1: No prior experience is needed for any of the three activities — every session opens with an on-site briefing. Minimum age for the quad is 16 with photo ID; children aged six and up can ride a camel with an adult.
guideSahara.practicalP2: Phone signal is intermittent once you're in the dunes — every guide carries a satellite messenger, and the base knows each group's route and expected return time.

guidePacking.title: What to pack for a night in the desert
guidePacking.lead: The real list, not a generic travel-blog one — what our guides actually recommend, and what we already provide on-site.
guidePacking.dayP1: Light, loose clothing, long sleeves and trousers rather than shorts — desert sun burns faster than it looks, even under cloud. Closed shoes are a must for walking on hot sand and for the quad.
guidePacking.dayP2: Sunglasses and high-factor sunscreen. We hand out a traditional chèche at the gate to protect your head, face and neck from dust and sun.
guidePacking.nightP1: A warm layer is essential — at minimum a sweater or light jacket. The day-to-night temperature swing in the desert is real, even at the height of the season: a hot afternoon turns into a cool evening the moment the sun goes down.
guidePacking.providedP1: Tents, bedding, and the desert chèche are provided at both the camp and on a bivouac — no need to bring your own sleeping or camping gear.
guidePacking.medP1: If you're on a medical treatment or have a dietary need, tell us when you book — we offer vegetarian, vegan, and gluten-free options, and our guides are briefed in advance on anything you tell us.
guidePacking.ctaSahara: Complete guide to the Sabria desert →

guideDjerbaTataouine.title: From Djerba to Tataouine and Chenini
guideDjerbaTataouine.lead: A route through island heritage, fortified granaries and hilltop settlements — with context from UNESCO and Tunisia's official tourism portal.
guideDjerbaTataouine.contextP1: Djerba is more than a beach departure point. UNESCO inscribed the island in 2023 for a dispersed settlement system shaped by scarce water, self-sufficiency and coexistence between communities. Menzels, rural mosques, market districts and a web of small roads form part of that wider landscape.
guideDjerbaTataouine.contextP2: South-west of the island, the terrain changes around Medenine and Tataouine. The official Tunisian tourism portal describes a region of rocky plateaus, ridge villages and ksour: fortified collective granaries whose individual storage chambers are known as ghorfas.
guideDjerbaTataouine.routeP1: Tataouine is a practical gateway rather than the whole story. Chenini and Douiret show how settlements occupied high ground and used partly rock-cut dwellings. Ksour such as Ouled Soltane and Haddada reveal another form: rows of ghorfas organised around a courtyard for storing harvests.
guideDjerbaTataouine.routeP2: Treat these places as inhabited heritage, not scenery. Dress for walking, ask before photographing people, use local guides where interpretation matters and leave time for the architecture, crafts and water-management systems that made settlement possible.
guideDjerbaTataouine.practicalP1: Official tourism information places Tataouine about 140 km by paved road from Djerba airport. Actual driving time depends on your start point, stops and road conditions; a circuit should therefore publish its own departure time rather than promise a universal duration.
guideDjerbaTataouine.practicalP2: Before departure, check current government travel advice and insurance conditions. Guidance for southern and border areas changes over time. Stay on the confirmed itinerary and never extend a heritage excursion into remote border territory on your own.

guideSabriaDouz.title: Sabria, Douz and Chott el-Jerid
guideSabriaDouz.lead: How the dunes, oasis villages and salt landscape fit together in the Kébili region.
guideSabriaDouz.contextP1: Tunisia's official tourism portal places Sabria, Nouil and El Faouar between the sandy desert and Chott el-Jerid. This matters: the region is not one uniform sea of dunes but a meeting of oasis agriculture, sandy villages, salt flats and the Grand Erg Oriental.
guideSabriaDouz.contextP2: Douz is the best-known gateway, while Sabria offers direct contact with the dunes and local camp life. Chott el-Jerid is a mostly dried salt basin crossed by a paved road; its glare and mirage effects are part of the landscape, but the crust should not be treated as an unrestricted driving surface.
guideSabriaDouz.routeP1: A useful itinerary gives each landscape its own time: the palm groves and market culture around Douz, a guided dune experience near Sabria, and a daylight crossing or viewpoint over Chott el-Jerid. Longer journeys can continue toward Tozeur's oasis landscape rather than forcing every stop into one day.
guideSabriaDouz.routeP2: The official portal identifies winter as an excellent season for Sahara exploration and autumn as another suitable period. Summer is primarily promoted for Tunisia's coast. In the desert, daily timing, shade, wind and temperature matter more than a generic monthly label.
guideSabriaDouz.practicalP1: The World Bank's Tunisia climate profile documents the country's strong heat exposure and regional variation. Use a current local forecast, carry water and sun protection, and accept route or timing changes made for weather conditions.
guideSabriaDouz.practicalP2: Remote desert travel is different from reaching an established camp by road. Use the booked guide and confirmed route, verify current official travel advice, and never assume that a visible track is public, safe or outside a restricted zone.

guideDunesCamp.title: A night at Dunes Insolites in Sabria
guideDunesCamp.lead: What the camp is, how you reach it and what to expect before you send a booking request.
guideDunesCamp.contextHeading: A camp beside the dunes, not an anonymous hotel
guideDunesCamp.contextP1: Dunes Insolites is based in Sabria in the Kébili region, about 30 km from Douz according to the camp's official presentation. Its identity is built around direct access to the desert, local hospitality and accommodation that keeps the atmosphere of a Saharan camp while providing essential facilities.
guideDunesCamp.contextP2: The public presentation lists furnished tents, hot showers, a café and restaurant, and an on-site team. The current booking catalogue can also distinguish tents, rooms and suites. Availability and the exact facilities of each option should always come from the live booking page rather than an old promotional description.
guideDunesCamp.routeP1: A typical stay begins with arrival instructions and installation, followed by time in the dunes around sunset. Dinner, mint tea, desert bread and an evening around the camp form the core experience described by Dunes Insolites; breakfast and departure follow the next morning when included in the selected formula.
guideDunesCamp.routeP2: The camp says it is reachable by a family car in normal conditions. That does not mean every visible track is suitable. Use the confirmed GPS point and approach, keep WhatsApp available and contact the team rather than choosing another route if wind or sand has altered access.
guideDunesCamp.practicalHeading: Choosing the right level of comfort
guideDunesCamp.practicalP1: Choose the established camp if toilets, showers and a defined accommodation category matter most. Choose a bivouac when the specific offer describes a simpler night farther into the dunes and that reduced level of infrastructure is part of what you want.
guideDunesCamp.practicalP2: Before confirmation, provide party size, children's ages, dietary or medical needs, transport choice and desired activities. This lets the server and local team validate a coherent stay instead of treating accommodation, pickup and activities as unrelated purchases.

guideDunesExperience.title: Activities, meals and evenings at Dunes Insolites
guideDunesExperience.lead: How to compose a stay around the camp without trying to fit every desert activity into one evening.
guideDunesExperience.contextHeading: The camp is the base of the experience
guideDunesExperience.contextP1: Dunes Insolites presents its activities as additions to a desert stay: camel or horse outings, quad, sandboarding, sunset photography, meals and bivouacs. The point is not to tick every box but to choose a pace that leaves time for the dunes and the camp itself.
guideDunesExperience.contextP2: Food is part of that rhythm. The official site highlights regional cooking, mint tea and bread prepared in hot sand and embers. Selected formulas determine whether dinner, breakfast or another meal is included, so the booking summary remains the final reference.
guideDunesExperience.routeP1: For a single night, one main activity before sunset is usually clearer than stacking several departures. A slower camel outing, a guided quad session or sandboarding each creates a different experience; return time, daylight and weather must remain compatible with dinner and installation.
guideDunesExperience.routeP2: A longer stay can separate active and quiet moments: one sunset activity, a full camp evening, then another outing the next morning or a bivouac extension. Private groups and events should be planned directly because transport, guides, meals and capacity must be coordinated together.
guideDunesExperience.practicalP1: Give the real ages and number of travellers, your arrival mode, preferred activity, dietary needs and any mobility or medical information relevant to participation. Guide and transport selections are validated together so contradictory options are not accepted.
guideDunesExperience.practicalP2: Prices and availability can vary by date, pricing unit and group size. The site recalculates selected services on the server; a screenshot, an old promotional page or a manually typed total is never the final booking price.

guideBivouacCamp.title: Bivouac or established camp in Sabria?
guideBivouacCamp.lead: Two ways to sleep in the desert, with very different levels of comfort and immersion.
guideBivouacCamp.contextHeading: The established camp: an equipped base
guideBivouacCamp.contextP1: Dunes Insolites is a fixed camp in Sabria. Its public information mentions fitted tents, toilets, hot showers, electricity and a team on site. This is often the simpler choice for a first desert night, a family or anyone who wants practical facilities nearby.
guideBivouacCamp.contextP2: A camp night still includes the essential moments: dune light, dinner, fire, the night sky and waking in the desert. Exact comfort depends on the category booked, so check the accommodation listing rather than relying on a general description.
guideBivouacCamp.routeHeading: The bivouac: travelling farther into the dunes
guideBivouacCamp.routeP1: The official bivouac starts from the camp with a guide, then combines travel through the dunes, a temporary camp, a meal and an overnight stay. It prioritises quiet and remoteness, with naturally lighter infrastructure than the fixed camp.
guideBivouacCamp.routeP2: Do not choose from a photograph alone. Ask how you travel, which equipment is supplied, what toilet arrangements exist, whether food and drinks are included and what alternative is planned if weather requires a change.
guideBivouacCamp.practicalHeading: Three questions that make the decision easier
guideBivouacCamp.practicalP1: Choose the camp if a shower, nearby toilets, a defined room or straightforward road access matter most. Choose the bivouac if you accept fewer facilities in exchange for more guided time away from the established camp.
guideBivouacCamp.practicalP2: Before confirmation, mention children, mobility, allergies, medication, electricity needs and sensitivity to heat or cold. The team can then recommend a suitable format instead of confirming an option that does not fit.

guideBedouinDinner.title: Bedouin dinner and sand bread in Sabria
guideBedouinDinner.lead: What turns a meal at camp into a complete desert evening.
guideBedouinDinner.contextHeading: The meal follows the changing light
guideBedouinDinner.contextP1: Dunes Insolites describes its dinner experience as a sequence of welcome, sunset, bread preparation, a meal under canvas, music and a campfire. It is therefore an evening experience, not simply a restaurant table moved onto the sand.
guideBedouinDinner.contextP2: Official pages mention Tunisian dishes, mint tea, fire cooking and sand bread. The menu can depend on the selected package and group; the booking confirmation, not an older promotional page, determines what is included on your date.
guideBedouinDinner.routeP1: Bread preparation connects cooking to the landscape: dough, embers and hot sand become a shared demonstration before dinner. Watching the technique and hearing its explanation gives the practice more meaning than treating it as a photo prop.
guideBedouinDinner.routeP2: After dinner, fire and music may extend the evening. Keep warm layers close, because comfort after sunset cannot be judged from the afternoon temperature.
guideBedouinDinner.practicalP1: Share allergies, religious restrictions, diets and children's needs before confirmation. Food prepared on site requires advance notice; a request made during service may be impossible to accommodate safely or properly.
guideBedouinDinner.practicalP2: Also check whether dinner belongs to the overnight package or is a separate activity, and which drinks and transport are included. The final summary should name each element clearly.

guideChooseActivity.title: Camel, quad bike or sandboard: what should you choose?
guideChooseActivity.lead: Compare each experience by pace and constraints, not only by its photograph.
guideChooseActivity.contextHeading: Three very different ways to read the dunes
guideChooseActivity.contextP1: A camel outing slows the pace and leaves room to observe the landscape. A quad bike covers more ground and puts driving and sensation at the centre. Sandboarding uses a selected slope and alternates climbing, practice and descent.
guideChooseActivity.contextP2: These activities are not interchangeable. Available time, fitness, participant age, wind and sand conditions may make one more appropriate than another. One well-timed activity is better than three rushed experiences.
guideChooseActivity.routeHeading: Match the activity to the time of day
guideChooseActivity.routeP1: A slow outing before sunset suits observation and photography. Quad riding requires the driver's full attention and follows a supervised route. Sandboarding works as a playful session on suitable dunes, following the guide's instructions.
guideChooseActivity.routeP2: For one night, generally choose one main activity before dinner. On a longer stay, separate motorised activities, walking and quiet periods so that the camp evening remains an experience in its own right.
guideChooseActivity.practicalP1: Give participants' ages, driving experience, mobility and relevant medical constraints. Ask who drives, what equipment is supplied, what the booked duration actually covers and whether conditions can require a change.
guideChooseActivity.practicalP2: Always follow the guide and remain on the planned route. Official pages describe organised activities from Dunes Insolites; they are not permission to take a vehicle alone onto any visible track.

guideFamilyStay.title: Planning a night in Sabria as a family
guideFamilyStay.lead: A straightforward stay when ages, pace and comfort needs are shared before arrival.
guideFamilyStay.contextP1: Advertised road access, toilets and an on-site team make the established camp easier to consider than a remote bivouac for many families. That still requires verification: ask for the real room or tent capacity, bedding arrangement and distance to facilities.
guideFamilyStay.contextP2: Age alone does not determine the right activity. A child may enjoy a short dune outing but tire during repeated transfers. Build the programme around sleep, meals and breaks instead of a checklist.
guideFamilyStay.routeHeading: A family programme with room to breathe
guideFamilyStay.routeP1: Arriving early enough to settle in, one suitable activity, sunset, dinner and the overnight stay already form a complete experience. Morning can stay unhurried for breakfast and a short walk near camp before departure.
guideFamilyStay.routeP2: Sand, sun and wind quickly change comfort. Carry water, sun protection, closed shoes, warm layers and a small light. Keep medicine and essential items with you rather than inside a vehicle that may be moved elsewhere.
guideFamilyStay.practicalHeading: What the team needs to know
guideFamilyStay.practicalP1: Send the number and ages of children, bed needs, allergies, food preferences, mobility and desired activities. Ask explicitly about any age or participation rules applying on the chosen date.
guideFamilyStay.practicalP2: Do not assume that a family photograph means every activity suits everyone. The team's confirmation should cover accommodation, food, transport and each selected activity separately.

guideDesertLight.title: Sunset, stars and photography in Sabria
guideDesertLight.lead: Enjoy the desert's best light without turning the entire evening into a photo shoot.
guideDesertLight.contextP1: Dunes Insolites highlights sunsets and photography in the dunes. The most useful advice is logistical: be settled and ready before the planned time, because reaching a viewpoint as the sun disappears leaves no margin.
guideDesertLight.contextP2: Low light reveals dune shapes and marks in the sand. A simple composition, level horizon and a few minutes without a camera often create better memories than constantly racing between dunes.
guideDesertLight.routeHeading: From twilight to the night sky
guideDesertLight.routeP1: Colour does not vanish immediately after sunset. Watch the twilight, then allow your eyes to adapt before observing stars. Keep bright screens away from the group and do not use flash near animals or other travellers.
guideDesertLight.routeP2: With a phone, stabilise it and avoid digital zoom. With a camera, bring a charged battery, protect equipment from sand and minimise lens changes when the wind rises.
guideDesertLight.practicalHeading: Respect the place and its people
guideDesertLight.practicalP1: Ask before photographing staff, guides, performers or other guests. A cultural evening is not a studio; some moments are better experienced without a screen or intrusive lighting.
guideDesertLight.practicalP2: Timing and visibility depend on season and weather. Ask for the recommended arrival time on your booking date and accept that cloud or wind may change the selected viewpoint.

guideDjerbaSabria.title: Djerba to Sabria with a night in the desert
guideDjerbaSabria.lead: A coherent route combining southern heritage, desert landscapes and an evening at Dunes Insolites.
guideDjerbaSabria.contextP1: Dunes Insolites' published tours connect Djerba, Matmata and Sabria with cultural stops and arrival at camp late in the day. Two days allow a meaningful introduction, but not every ksar, oasis and village in the South without spending most of the journey inside a vehicle.
guideDjerbaSabria.contextP2: Choose one principal axis: Matmata and its landscapes, or Tataouine and the ksour, followed by the Sabria night. The exact route should be confirmed with the driver or guide according to departure point, season and opening hours.
guideDjerbaSabria.routeP1: Day one should aim for an arrival early enough to settle in and see sunset. Adding one final stop after the programme is already delayed sacrifices the moment for which the desert night was selected.
guideDjerbaSabria.routeP2: Day two can return to Djerba by a different route or include one principal stop. Keep margin for breakfast, road conditions and breaks; an arrival estimate with no buffer is not a guarantee.
guideDjerbaSabria.practicalP1: Check pickup place, vehicle type, luggage allowance, meals, admissions and guide language. If reaching camp independently, request the GPS point and latest arrival time separately.
guideDjerbaSabria.practicalP2: Inspiration pages describe examples. Only your booking summary confirms the stops actually included. Review current official travel advice before departure and do not alter the route toward isolated areas on your own.
